A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ApolloPFN. All 16 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including appendices A–C and A–F respectively, are readable. Text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting results on M5, electricity prices, and univariate benchmarks, alongside graph-generation and architectural ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds air-quality and solar-generation results, a data-generation ablation, covariate robustness tests, and prediction-interval calibration analyses.

M1.justification: The PFN objective, SRNGN algorithm, temporally correlated root excitation, separable attention, rotary and absolute positional encodings, and full horizon attention are retained. v2 reorganizes their explanation and discloses implementation details without establishing a different proposed procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds daily UCI Air Quality CO forecasting and hourly solar-generation forecasting with weather covariates (Table 3 and Appendix C.3). Appendix E.1 also introduces M5 scenarios with corrupted or irrelevant exogenous inputs. Existing M5, electricity-market, and univariate benchmark coverage remains.

E2.justification: AutoARIMAX and Prophet are added to the existing M5 and electricity comparisons, substantially broadening comparisons beyond foundation models. The four original foundation-model comparators remain, and the univariate comparator set is unchanged. Chronos-2 is discussed but explicitly left for future evaluation.

E3.justification: The stated training sample range changes from 34–512 in v1 to 10–512 context samples in v2. Added experiments introduce 37 air-quality windows with 14-day horizons, 51 solar windows with 24-hour horizons, controlled 50% covariate perturbations, and multi-level coverage evaluation. Newly documented settings for retained benchmarks do not establish that their protocols changed or experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Figure 5 ablates temporal root excitation and SRNGN separately. Appendix E adds robustness tests distinguishing corrupted informative covariates from Gaussian, autoregressive, and Fourier distractors, plus quantitative calibration comparisons against TabPFN-TS. Earlier convergence and architectural ablations remain as Figures 4 and 6.

E5.justification: Table 6 newly documents predictive uncertainty estimation, including 100 trajectories for Sundial and 100 Monte Carlo samples for Moirai. Appendix E.2 adds coverage reporting at 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80% prediction intervals. These additions concern predictive uncertainty; neither version reports repeated-training seed counts, significance tests, or confidence intervals on benchmark scores.

E6.justification: M5 and electricity scores are extensively revised. For example, ApolloPFN's state-level M5(D-B) RMSSE changes from 0.580 to 0.500; NP(24) ApolloPFN/TabPFN-TS sCRPS changes from 0.038/0.048 to 0.019/0.018, reversing their ranking. These are revised reported results, not established same-setting gains. v2 adds domain, ablation, robustness, and calibration outcomes; the original univariate table is numerically unchanged.

T1.justification: The Bayesian predictive formulation, graph algorithms, attention equations, positional encodings, and embedding mathematics are retained. v2 restates the objective using forecasting notation and relocates metric definitions, without adding substantive theoretical assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

C1.justification: The two central contributions—temporal synthetic priors and time-aware architecture—remain. However, the abstract and conclusion replace broad state-of-the-art claims with improvements over evaluated baselines. The introduction also drops v1's categorical claim that existing PFNs are unsuitable as time-series foundation models, describing limitations in particular forecasting settings instead.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of robustness and calibration: it distinguishes tolerance of irrelevant features from degradation when informative covariates are weakened, and interprets gradual degradation as resistance to spurious signals. It also attributes SRNGN gains under fixed budgets to covariate–target relationship complexity. Existing limitations concerning quadratic attention, scarce context, and synthetic-prior coverage remain.

D1.justification: Expanded Appendix C documents evaluation windows, horizons, aggregation, preprocessing, and future-covariate selection. New Appendix D and Table 6 specify model dimensions, checkpoints, baseline implementations, optimizer, precision, quantile estimation, and checkpoint averaging. Dataset access descriptions change from GIFT-Eval/LOTSA to Monash, EPFtoolbox, and fev-bench. ApolloPFN code is identified as internal, not newly released.

R1.justification: v2 adds Chronos-2, Monash, fev-bench, new dataset references, and statistical-baseline citations, while removing GIFT-Eval and several background citations. The introduction more cautiously distinguishes corpus-pretrained forecasting models from PFNs and acknowledges both approaches' strengths. The central positioning as a temporally adapted PFN remains.

P1.justification: The introduction and method exposition are substantially rewritten. The standalone Background section is integrated into the ApolloPFN description, metrics move to Appendix B, and architecture details move from Appendix A to F. Evaluation and appendix organization are extensively revised, alongside authorship and publication-header changes.

P2.justification: v2 adds a detailed synthetic-data workflow diagram, a data-component ablation plot, and tables for new domains, implementation details, robustness, and calibration. Existing comparison tables gain rows and change ordering; retained figures are relocated or renumbered. The expanded author block and journal formatting also materially alter layout.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited reproducibility documentation and lack of systematic tests supporting robustness and calibration claims. Appendices C–E, statistical comparators, and additional domains make the evidence more auditable and expose applicability boundaries, while the main claims become more qualified. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, notably the approximately 5.6% sCRPS improvement claimed in Section 4.2, which is not readily reconciled with Tables 2–3.
